_comment: Every externally sourced figure this contribution publishes, with where it came from and when it was read at source. It exists because one of them was wrong. The README said England recorded 18.7% persistent absence in 2024/25; that number appears nowhere in the DfE release and the published rate is 17.63%. It was caught by reading the primary source rather than by any check, which is the kind of luck this file replaces. tests/test_claims.py fails if the README publishes a figure that is not here, or publishes one of these with a different value. Every figure either appears inside its own quote or carries `quote_is`, saying why it cannot: a table cell with no sentence behind it, or a subtraction done here. Four of thirteen quotes did not contain their figure and nothing checked that, which is what `tests/test_claims.py::test_every_sourced_figure_is_in_its_own_quote_or_says_why_not` now does.

figures.claim: United States students chronically absent in the 2021-22 school year, which the publisher defines as missing at least 10 percent of school days
figures.quote: Over 14 million students nationwide during the 2021–22 school year were chronically absent. This means that they missed at least 10 percent of school days—equivalent to approximately 18 days in the year.
figures.note: The publisher gives no dated byline on the page, so `published` is the year IES attributes to the resource collection rather than a date the page states. `read_at_source` is the date the sentence above was read from it. The figure is a floor: the source says "Over 14 million", so the value is written as "14 million" and every surface that shows it says "more than" or "over".

figures.claim: persistent absence rate across the autumn and spring terms of 2024/25 in England
figures.quote: The number of pupils persistently absent decreased from 1.42 million (19.23%) across autumn and spring terms 2023/24 to 1.29 million (17.63%) in the same period of 2024/25. This remains above the pre-pandemic rate of 10.53% in autumn and spring terms 2018/19.

figures.claim: the same rate a year earlier, autumn and spring terms 2023/24
figures.quote: decreased from 1.42 million (19.23%) across autumn and spring terms 2023/24

figures.claim: the pre-pandemic rate, autumn and spring terms 2018/19
figures.quote: This remains above the pre-pandemic rate of 10.53% in autumn and spring terms 2018/19.

figures.claim: share of the United States population aged 5 and over who spoke only English at home, 2018-2022 American Community Survey five-year estimates
figures.quote: 78.3% of the population age 5 and over spoke only English at home

figures.claim: the remainder, who speak a language other than English at home
figures.quote: derived: 100% minus the 78.3% who spoke only English at home
figures.quote_is: derived, and it says so in the quote: 100% minus the 78.3% the publisher states. The subtraction is here rather than in the source, which is why the figure is not in its own quote.

figures.claim: Operating public elementary and secondary schools in the United States, school year 2023-24
figures.publisher: National Center for Education Statistics, Common Core of Data
figures.quote: Public Elementary/Secondary School Universe Survey, 2023-24 Final Version 1a
figures.note: The count of schools, not of districts. NCES publishes two district counts for the same year under two definitions: 13,303 regular school districts in Table 1 and 19,186 operating districts in Table 2, the wider one including charter agencies, supervisory unions and service agencies. The narrower one is used here because it is the count of bodies that run an attendance office.
figures.quote_is: a table cell, not a sentence. No prose in this source states the count: it is the total row of the school universe table, column "Total", row "United States". The quote below is the table's own title, which is what a reader needs to find the right table, and it is named as a title rather than offered as a sentence containing the figure.

figures.claim: Operating regular school districts in the United States, school year 2023-24
figures.publisher: National Center for Education Statistics, Common Core of Data
figures.quote: Operational and student membership status of public elementary and secondary schools and agencies, by type
figures.note: See the note on 99,297. The wider NCES figure for the same year is 19,186 and is a different definition of district, not a correction to this one.
figures.quote_is: a table cell, not a sentence, in the same way as us-public-schools: the "Regular school districts" row of the agency universe table, United States total. The quote below is the table's own title.

figures.claim: Total purchase cost approved by one North Carolina school district for its annual PowerSchool contract renewal, 2024-25, paid from the capital outlay technology budget
figures.publisher: Chapel Hill-Carrboro City Schools Board of Education, Agenda Abstract, 15 August 2024
figures.quote: The total purchase cost of $157,664 will be paid from funds allocated in the Article 46 Technology Budget contained in the FY 2024-25 Capital Outlay Fund.
figures.note: A bundle, not a bare student-information-system licence: it covers the core SIS plus Enrollment Registration with additional languages, Enrollment School Choice, PowerPack, Unified Talent Professional Learning, State Data Validation and Naviance. One district's price, on the record, rather than a market average. Divided by the district's enrolment it is about $13.89 a student a year, which is arithmetic and is labelled as such wherever it appears.
figures.quote_is: a sentence, from the FINANCIAL IMPACT paragraph of the agenda abstract. The resolution on the same page repeats the figure: "the Board of Education approves the PowerSchool contract for 2024-25 for the amount of $157,664". The quote here used to be "the annual renewal of the PowerSchool, LLC Contract for 2024-25", which carries no amount, so the largest dollar figure in this entry was the one a reader could not check against its own quote.

figures.claim: students enrolled in Chapel Hill-Carrboro City Schools, North Carolina, in the 2024-25 school year, which is the year of the system renewal priced above it
figures.publisher: National Center for Education Statistics, Common Core of Data, US Department of Education
figures.quote: District Details (2024-2025 school year; Fiscal data from 2022-2023) [...] Chapel Hill-Carrboro City Schools [...] Total Students: 11,353
figures.note: This figure replaces one that was wrong in two ways, and both are the kind this register exists to catch. It said 11,386 students, citing a US News district page. 11,386 is a real number, but it is the 2023-24 CCD year, confirmed against the Urban Institute's mirror of the same federal data (year 2023 returns enrollment 11386 and 21 schools; year 2024 returns 11353 and 20 schools). And the URL cited carried the wrong district id (102495): two independent fetchers both return a page titled Howells-Dodge Consolidated Schools, a 297-student district in Nebraska, at HTTP 200 with no redirect. The correct US News id is 111172. The federal source is cited instead of the aggregator, and the year now matches the renewal it is divided into. The district's own site says only "more than 11,000 students", and North Carolina's ADM report is behind a dashboard that serves nothing without JavaScript, so neither can carry this claim.

figures.claim: Texas Basic Allotment per student in average daily attendance, school year 2025-26
figures.quote: the golden penny yield is calculated as the Basic Allotment (BA) of $6,215 multiplied by 0.02084, and the copper penny yield is determined by multiplying the Basic Allotment by 0.0008
figures.note: An annual figure per student in attendance, not a per-absence figure. Dividing it by an instructional-day count gives roughly $35.51 at 175 days or $34.53 at 180, which is arithmetic on a divisor that varies by district size and year, and is labelled arithmetic wherever it appears. Texas raised the allotment from $6,160 through HB2 of the 89th Legislature.
figures.quote_is: a sentence, from the section on Tier Two yields. The letter states the allotment while deriving something else from it, which is why the quote reads as arithmetic. It replaces the letter's title, which was the previous quote and named no figure.

figures.claim: US dollars, median annual wage for secretaries and administrative assistants in educational services, which is the grade of the work this app takes off a school office desk
figures.quote: In May 2025, the median annual wages for secretaries and administrative assistants in some of the top industries in which they worked were as follows: [...] Educational services; state, local, and private 48,980
figures.note: The industry figure, not the whole-occupation median, which is $48,310 on the same page. A reader who checks only the summary block finds the smaller number and concludes the citation is wrong; the industry table is where this one is. `published` is the page's own last-modified date. The app divides it by 2,080 hours, which reads a ten-month school contract as cheaper per hour than it is, and a salary excludes the benefits paid on top: both errors make the desk look cheap and this app look worse.

figures.claim: US dollars, median annual wage for school and career counselors and advisors in local elementary and secondary schools, which is the grade the work this app creates lands on
figures.quote: In May 2025, the median annual wages for school and career counselors and advisors in some of the top industries in which they worked were as follows: Elementary and secondary schools; local $77,800
figures.note: Added because a district buyer read the run and found the arithmetic priced the labour removed and not the labour added. A safeguarding callback goes to the designated safeguarding lead, a post a US district staffs with a counsellor or an administrator. Counsellors are the cheaper of the two, so this understates the added cost in the same direction the 2,080 hours understates the saved one. It is 1.59 times the desk wage, which is why the run's ceiling falls from $0.59 to $0.35 a call once the added work is paid for, per attempt billed on both halves of that subtraction.

figures.claim: California students in the 2023-24 eligible cumulative enrolment, which the publisher defines as non-exempt students expected to attend more than 30 days. This is the denominator the absence-volume figure in docs/what-a-pilot-would-look-like.md is divided by
figures.quote_is: a row of the Report Totals table, under the headers Eligible Cumulative Enrollment, Count of Students with One or More Absences, Average Days Absent, Excused Absences, Unexcused Absences, Out-of-School Suspension Absences and Incomplete Independent Study Absences. The page renders those cells adjacent with no separator, so the spaces in the quote are added to make the row readable and no digit is changed. Read at the State report level on purpose: the page's own footnote says charter school data are removed by default from district-level reports “including the associated state and county Report Totals”, so a Statewide row read off a district-level page is a different population and gives 5,236,744.
figures.note: The publisher gives no dated byline, so `published` is the academic year CDE attributes the collection to rather than a date the page states. The page names its own provenance: “Absenteeism and Cumulative Enrollment data were submitted and certified by LEAs and/or charter schools as part of the annual CALPADS EOY 3 submission.” Cumulative enrolment is larger than census-day enrolment, which makes it the conservative choice for a per-student rate.

figures.claim: California students who missed one or more days of school between 1 July 2023 and 30 June 2024. The publisher calculates Total Days Absent from this count and not from enrolment, so the derivation has to as well
figures.quote_is: a row of the Report Totals table, under the headers Eligible Cumulative Enrollment, Count of Students with One or More Absences, Average Days Absent, Excused Absences, Unexcused Absences, Out-of-School Suspension Absences and Incomplete Independent Study Absences. The page renders those cells adjacent with no separator, so the spaces in the quote are added to make the row readable and no digit is changed. Read at the State report level on purpose: the page's own footnote says charter school data are removed by default from district-level reports “including the associated state and county Report Totals”, so a Statewide row read off a district-level page is a different population and gives 5,236,744.

figures.claim: average days absent in California in 2023-24, which the publisher defines as Total Days Absent divided by the count of students with one or more absences
figures.quote_is: a row of the Report Totals table, under the headers Eligible Cumulative Enrollment, Count of Students with One or More Absences, Average Days Absent, Excused Absences, Unexcused Absences, Out-of-School Suspension Absences and Incomplete Independent Study Absences. The page renders those cells adjacent with no separator, so the spaces in the quote are added to make the row readable and no digit is changed. Read at the State report level on purpose: the page's own footnote says charter school data are removed by default from district-level reports “including the associated state and county Report Totals”, so a Statewide row read off a district-level page is a different population and gives 5,236,744.
figures.note: Shown to one decimal, which is the only rounding in the derivation that moves the answer. Taking 13.05 and 13.15 as the bounds moves the derived rate from 27.6 to 27.9 per 1,000, so the published figure is given as about 28 and the range in the document is wider than the rounding.

figures.claim: the share of all California absence days in 2023-24 that were unexcused, which the publisher defines as days a student was absent without a valid excuse, excluding out-of-school suspension
figures.quote_is: a row of the Report Totals table, under the headers Eligible Cumulative Enrollment, Count of Students with One or More Absences, Average Days Absent, Excused Absences, Unexcused Absences, Out-of-School Suspension Absences and Incomplete Independent Study Absences. The page renders those cells adjacent with no separator, so the spaces in the quote are added to make the row readable and no digit is changed. Read at the State report level on purpose: the page's own footnote says charter school data are removed by default from district-level reports “including the associated state and county Report Totals”, so a Statewide row read off a district-level page is a different population and gives 5,236,744.
figures.note: The publisher's glossary is the reason this figure is an upper bound on what this software would call about: “Unexcused Absences are reported for the days a student was absent without a valid excuse and does not include students who are absent due to an out-of-school suspension or who attended in-school suspension.” Absent without a valid excuse is wider than absent with no reason given, because a parent who telephones to report a holiday or a missed bus has explained the absence and it is still unexcused.

figures.claim: days of instruction a California school district is penalised for offering less than, used as the length of the school year the per-day figure divides by
figures.quote: and that offers less than 180 days of instruction or, in multitrack year-round schools, fewer than the number of days required in subdivision (a) of this section
figures.note: Education Code 46200, amended by Stats. 2013, Ch. 357. It is a statutory floor rather than a measured average: the Superintendent withholds funding from a district offering fewer days, so 180 is the shortest year a district will normally run. The document shows the figure at 175 and 185 days as well, because the year length is a larger lever on the answer than any rounding in the source data.
